title: An Astronaut Spots 'Moon Rock' on Earth
summary:
When you look at the Moon, you can see bright areas called highlands. Much of that brightness comes from a rock called anorthosite. Now an astronaut has taken a picture of a big patch of this rock on Earth.

On August 28, 2026, an astronaut on the International Space Station photographed it in southern Madagascar. Madagascar is an island country near Africa. From space, the rock looks like a bright circle. It covers about 40 square miles.

Anorthosite forms when melted rock cools slowly underground. That gives its crystals time to grow big. Scientists think this patch is at least 600 million years old.

Long ago, big pieces of land crashed together to make a giant supercontinent called Gondwana. The heat and pressure bent the rocks around this patch.

Studying Moon-like rocks on Earth can help scientists learn how the Moon formed.
why_it_matters: You can see the Moon's bright highlands at night, and rocks on Earth help explain what they are made of.
